p152.lead: Jairus’s daughter and Veronica, the feeding of the five thousand, the only planned nature miracle, and a crown refused: the paper in which popular acclaim reaches its peak and then breaks.

p152.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p152.s0.h: Introduction — Not the Touch, but Faith
p152.s0.b0: After the news of Amos’s cure spread, a great crowd waited on the Capernaum shore, among them new observers sent by the Sanhedrin. Jairus, a ruler of the synagogue, fell at Jesus’ feet on behalf of his dying only daughter, and Jesus answered that he would go with him. On the way a woman secretly touched the hem of his garment and was healed of a long-standing hemorrhage.

p152.s0.b1.q: It was her faith and not her touch that made her whole.

p152.s0.b2: Jesus had a reason for calling this woman, Veronica of Caesarea-Philippi, forward: to correct two errors that might linger in her mind or in the minds of the witnesses. Touching his garment was merely the superstitious part of her belief; with the faith she had, it was enough to approach the Master’s person.

head: The error to be corrected
The truth Jesus wanted known
rows: That her fearful attempt to steal her cure had been honored
He called her forward openly and praised her faith; there was no need to hide
The superstition that touching his garment had healed her
Her pure and living faith laid hold on creative power

p152.s0.b4: This paper covers the peak and turning point of the Galilean ministry. Jesus’ fame as a healer reaches its height, and the feeding of the five thousand raises popular enthusiasm to its highest pitch, but when Jesus refuses a crown, his following shrinks rapidly. Following this course, readers can compare what Jesus wanted with what the people wanted.
p152.s1.h: I. At Jairus’s House — A Girl Awakened, and a Life That Cannot Be Repeated
p152.s1.b0: Before they reached the house a servant came to say the girl was dead, but Jesus said, “⟦Q 152:1.1⟧Fear not; only believe.⟦/Q⟧” He put the mourners out, went in with the parents and three apostles, took the girl by the hand, and told her to awake and arise. Then he directed that she be given something to eat, for she had long been without food.
p152.s1.b1: Jesus explained to the family and the apostles that the girl had been in a coma following a long fever and that he had merely aroused her. But being miracle-minded, they all believed he had raised her from the dead. Here the gap shows between Jesus, who honestly stated the facts, and followers eager to ascribe yet another wonder to him.
p152.s1.b2: As he left Jairus’s house, two blind men led by a dumb boy followed him, crying out for healing. Everywhere the sick were waiting for him, and the Master looked much worn; his friends feared he would teach and heal to the point of collapse. This weariness forms the background for his departure across the lake in the next section.
p152.s1.b3: The narrator says that neither science nor religion can ever check up on these events, because such a situation can never occur again anywhere in Nebadon: a being in mortal flesh embodying creative energy together with spiritual endowments. Yet this does not close the door on believers today.

p152.s1.b4.q: Though the Master is absent as a material being, he is present as a spiritual influence in the hearts of men.

p152.s2.h: II. Feeding the Five Thousand — The First and Only Planned Nature Miracle
p152.s2.b0: Jesus crossed to a park south of Bethsaida-Julias to rest, but the people hired boats and walked around the lake after him. From a thousand on Sunday the crowd grew to about five thousand by Wednesday noon, and the food they had brought ran out. Meanwhile it was quietly whispered that this secluded spot was the place to crown Jesus king, and a young evangelist named Joab led the plot.

Apostles
rows: In favor

Noncommittal
Matthew, Philip, the Alpheus twins

p152.s2.b2: Philip had provided only a three days’ supply of food for Jesus and the twelve, kept by the Mark lad, their chore boy. His reckoning that two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough was realistic. But Jesus’ question was, “⟦Q 152:2.6⟧can you not feed them?⟦/Q⟧” He wanted the apostles to take the crowd’s need as their own responsibility rather than send it away.
p152.s2.b3: Philip and Andrew proposed dismissing the multitude; Andrew in particular feared the king plot might materialize. Jesus said the people were like sheep without a shepherd and that he wished to feed them, and the Mark lad brought the remaining five barley loaves and two dried fishes. The people sat down in companies of a hundred; Jesus gave thanks and the food was distributed; all ate and were filled, and the fragments filled twelve baskets.

p152.s2.b4.q: And this is the first and only nature miracle which Jesus performed as a result of his conscious preplanning.

p152.s2.b5: The narrator briefly describes how it happened: Michael multiplied the food elements as he always does, except that the time factor and the visible life channel were eliminated. Later Jesus told the apostles that he yielded to his sympathy for the multitude only after he had ascertained that it was according to the Father’s will.
p152.s3.h: III. The King-Making Episode — A Crowd with Full Stomachs
p152.s3.b0: To the well-fed multitude, this seemed the fulfillment of the long-held expectation that the Messiah would bestow the bread of life. The idea of making Jesus king spread through the crowd like a contagion that needed no further direction, and the people rose as one man, shouting to make him king.

p152.s3.b1.q: In the eyes of these simple-minded people the power to feed carried with it the right to rule.

p152.s3.b2: Jesus stepped onto a huge stone and told them they meant well but were shortsighted and material-minded. They wanted him as king not because their souls had been lighted with a great truth but because their stomachs had been filled with bread. The kingdom of heaven is a spiritual brotherhood with no material throne, and its Ruler is the Father.

p152.s3.b3.q: If you must have a king, let the Father of lights be enthroned in the heart of each of you as the spirit Ruler of all things.

p152.s3.b4: The multitude went away stunned and disheartened, and many followed him no more from that day. The apostles stood speechless by the baskets of fragments; only the Mark lad spoke, saying that he had refused to be their king. Before going alone into the hills, Jesus told Andrew to pray with his brethren, especially for Simon Peter.
p152.s4.h: IV–V. Simon Peter’s Night Vision; Back in Bethsaida
p152.s4.b0: Rowing without the Master against a contrary wind that night, Peter, the most downcast of all, fell into an exhausted sleep. He dreamed that he saw Jesus walking on the sea, that he himself walked on the water, began to sink, and cried out to be saved. Acting out the dream, he actually stepped overboard and awoke as his companions pulled him from the water.
p152.s4.b1: To Peter the experience was always real. He only partially convinced Mark, while Luke, who searched carefully into these matters, concluded it was a vision and left it out of his narrative. The text in effect invites readers to distinguish the sincerity of an experience from the factuality of an event.
p152.s4.b2: Jesus, meanwhile, had walked back to Bethsaida during the night with the Mark lad. Of the five thousand, only about five hundred kept following him. He gathered the apostles and their associates, reminded them of the psalmists’ words of trust, and rebuked their material motives.

p152.s4.b3.q: Of the five thousand who were miraculously fed, and who, when their stomachs were full and their hearts empty, would have made him king, only about five hundred persisted in following after him.

p152.s4.b4.q: And now do you all see that the working of miracles and the performance of material wonders will not win souls for the spiritual kingdom?

p152.s4.b5: The narrator judges that the miracle did nothing for halfhearted believers but brought to a head the miracle-seeking and king-craving tendencies of Jesus’ closest followers. It marked the turning point into the last year of his ministry, given to proclaiming divine sonship, spiritual liberty, and eternal salvation.
p152.s5.h: VI. At Gennesaret — Appeal to the Spirit
p152.s5.b0: While resting at Gennesaret, Jesus held conferences with the apostles every afternoon. Meanwhile his open followers, more than fifty thousand in Galilee alone, shrank in less than a month to fewer than five hundred. Jesus wanted the apostles to experience for themselves how fickle popular acclaim is, so that later they would not rely on transient religious hysteria.

p152.s5.b1.q: It requires time for men and women to effect radical and extensive changes in their basic and fundamental concepts of social conduct, philosophic attitudes, and religious convictions.

p152.s5.b2: Retelling the parable of the sower, Jesus distinguished three ways of appealing to people. Emotion is only a technique for arresting attention; the quickened mind is the gateway to the soul; and true transformation of character comes when the spiritual nature within responds to truth.

p152.s5.b4.q: it is only by making your appeal to the spirit which lives within the human mind that you can hope to achieve lasting success

p152.s5.b5: Preparing them for the crisis only days away, Jesus explained that the Jerusalem leaders would conspire with Herod Antipas to destroy them. The apostles began to realize that he would not sit on David’s throne and that spiritual truth is not advanced by material wonders. Recognizing that the feeding of the five thousand was the height of popular acclaim readied them for the sifting and adversity to come.
p152.s6.h: VII. At Jerusalem — The Approaching Crisis
p152.s6.b0: Jesus went to Jerusalem quietly with only the twelve and forbade any teaching or preaching during this Passover. There the apostles learned how bitter feeling toward their Master had become, and they returned convinced that a crisis was impending.

p152.s6.b2: Jesus sent Andrew to ask permission to speak in the Capernaum synagogue, knowing well that it would be the last time he would be allowed to speak there. So the paper ends with the Capernaum crisis of the next paper standing at the door.
p152.s7.b0: Paper 152 shows both the height of Jesus’ popularity and its collapse. He refused the crown the crowd wanted and asked that the throne of each heart be given to the Father. The lesson that miracles can fill stomachs but cannot win souls is sharp for readers today who measure faith by results or by the intensity of experience.

p152.s7.b2: In the next paper, Paper 153, “The Crisis at Capernaum,” Jesus preaches in the synagogue on the bread of life, and many of his followers leave him.
p153.lead: The bread-of-life sermon in the Capernaum synagogue and the disputes that followed: the paper in which popular acclaim ebbs away and those who remain stand at the parting of the ways.

p153.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p153.s0.h: Introduction — The Lull Before the Storm
p153.s0.b0: From Friday evening, the day they reached Bethsaida after returning from Jerusalem, through Sabbath morning, Jesus was deep in thought; he ate almost nothing and said little. The apostles and their associates gathered in small groups about the house, in the garden, and along the seashore, and an uneasy foreboding hung over them all. This paper records the epoch-making sermon Jesus preached that afternoon in the Capernaum synagogue and the events that ran on into that night.
p153.s0.b1: The narrative pauses to note how each apostle reacted, in his own way, to the same tension. Their varied responses mirror their temperaments and their expectations, and a reader may find among them a face that looks much like his or her own.

p153.s1.h: I. The Setting of the Stage — The Turning-Point Crisis
p153.s1.b0: At three o’clock in the afternoon, in the new synagogue where Jairus presided, sat fifty-three Pharisees and Sadducees from Jerusalem, more than thirty leaders of the neighboring synagogues, and the official observers of Herod Antipas. This orthodox vanguard, acting under orders from the Sanhedrin, had come to inaugurate open warfare. Jesus knew it, and he chose boldly to assume the offensive.
p153.s1.b1: The text calls this sermon the outward turning of the tide of popular fame. From then on the work of the kingdom would be more and more concerned with winning lasting spiritual converts rather than great crowds. The crisis, moreover, spanned different stretches of time for Jesus and for his apostles.

head: Whose crisis
Began
Ended
rows: Jesus’ earth life
The feeding of the five thousand
This synagogue sermon
The apostles’ lives
This synagogue sermon
A whole year later, with the Master’s trial and crucifixion

p153.s1.b3: Just before the sermon, one question filled the minds of everyone in the synagogue: why had he so deliberately turned back the tide of popular enthusiasm? The feeding of the five thousand had made the greatest appeal to the Jewish idea of the Messiah, but his prompt refusal to be made king had immediately offset that advantage. Disappointment grew into unconscious opposition and eventually into hatred, and it was after this sermon that Judas Iscariot first consciously thought of deserting.

p153.s1.b4.q: Jesus fully understood how men prepare themselves for the decisions of a crisis and the performance of sudden deeds of courageous choosing by the slow process of the reiterated choosing between the recurring situations of good and evil.

p153.s1.b5: This insight reminds us that great decisions are not made overnight. Jesus put his apostles through repeated rehearsals in disappointment, trusting that in the final test their habitual spirit reactions would carry them through. Meanwhile, despite the long and earnest pleading of the Jerusalem leaders, Jairus kept his word.

p153.s1.b6.q: I have granted this request, and I will not violate my word.

p153.s2.h: II. The Epochal Sermon — The Bread of Life
p153.s2.b0: Jesus read from Deuteronomy the curses that would overtake a disobedient people, and from Jeremiah the story of the prophet let down into a filthy dungeon for his warnings. If that was what they did to a prophet who warned of political downfall, he asked, what would they do to a teacher who warned of spiritual doom? He told them they already had sufficient evidence to decide, and he called on them to choose that very day whom they would serve.
p153.s2.b1: Jesus said that he had left them undisturbed in their positions of influence and power and had only proclaimed new liberty for man’s fear-ridden soul. His purpose was to reveal the Father and to establish the spiritual brotherhood of the sons of God. And the Father had granted them, beyond material wonders, the more evidential signs of spiritual transformation and regeneration.
p153.s2.b2: He then laid bare the motives of those who had pursued him across the lake. They had come not for truth or service but for more bread for which they had not labored, because they had long been taught that the Messiah would make life pleasant and easy.

p153.s2.b3.q: I have come to proclaim spiritual liberty, teach eternal truth, and foster living faith.

p153.s2.b4: Pointing to the pot of manna carved on the lintel of the synagogue, Jesus said that the manna their forefathers ate was the bread of earth. The bread of heaven is that which comes down from God and gives eternal life—and he himself is that bread.

head: Food that perishes
The bread of life
rows: Manna in the wilderness — the bread of earth
The bread of heaven that comes down from God
Those who ate it are dead
Whoever eats it shall never die in spirit
Bread given yesterday for the body
Bread offered today for the hungry soul
The bread of ease, gained without labor
Eternal life for all who behold the Son and believe him

p153.s2.b6: When a teacher from the Sanhedrin asked how the son of Joseph the carpenter could have come down from heaven, the synagogue began to murmur. Jesus asked for patience and answered that he was all that they said, and more.

p153.s2.b7.q: the truth never suffers from honest examination.

p153.s2.b8.q: And this bread of life which I give to all who will receive is my own living and combined nature.

p153.s3.h: III. The After Meeting — Not Hands but Hearts
p153.s3.b0: Even after the congregation was dismissed, the questions went on for more than three hours. One Pharisee climbed onto a lampstand and mockingly asked how Jesus could give them his flesh to eat and his blood to drink. Jesus explained that he had not been teaching about literal flesh and blood, but about a reality of experience: the Word of God bestowed in the flesh and a life lived in subjection to the Father’s will.

p153.s3.b1.q: You cannot eat my flesh nor can you drink my blood, but you can become one in spirit with me even as I am one in spirit with the Father.

p153.s3.b2: A Jerusalem spy then accused him of breaking the tradition of washing hands. Jesus pointed to the tradition that let undutiful children say the money that should have helped their parents had been “⟦Q 153:3.3⟧given to God⟦/Q⟧,” and he charged them with making void the commandment of God by their own tradition. The spies had raised the question because a saying of Jesus had been reported to them.

p153.s3.b3.q: Salvation is a matter of clean hearts rather than of clean hands.

head: What does not defile a man
What defiles a man
rows: What enters the body by the mouth
The evil that originates in the heart and comes out in words and deeds
What reaches the mind through the eyes and ears
Evil thoughts; wicked projects of murder, theft, and adulteries
Bread eaten with ceremonially unclean hands
Jealousy, pride, anger, revenge, railings, and false witness

p153.s3.b5: Even the apostles did not grasp his meaning, and Peter asked him to explain, lest some of the hearers be unnecessarily offended. Jesus replied that no one can compel men to love the truth, so they should turn their attention to those who would know it. He added the warning that when the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit. For anyone worn out with trying to persuade others, these words show where to spend one’s strength.
p153.s3.b6: The text adds that such beliefs, once they become part of one’s religion, are hard to get away from. Even Peter remained in bondage to fears about things clean and unclean until many years later, when he was finally delivered through a vivid dream. Knowing that an open rupture with these leaders could no longer be prevented, Jesus spoke out with less reserve and exposed the folly of the whole system of the oral law.
p153.s4.h: IV. Last Words in the Synagogue — Our Choices Make Us
p153.s4.b0: A Pharisee brought forward a youth possessed of an unruly and rebellious spirit, and Jesus, moved with compassion, took him by the hand and sent the spirit out. The text explains that this was the first case in which Jesus really cast an evil spirit out of a human being, and that such possession became forever impossible after Pentecost, when the Master’s spirit was poured out upon all flesh. The Pharisees then charged that he did these things by the power of Beelzebub.
p153.s4.b1: Jesus answered that a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand, and he solemnly warned those who would knowingly and with premeditated malice ascribe the works of God to devils. Such persons will never seek nor receive forgiveness, and so they reject divine forgiveness themselves. He then made plain the weight of choice with the figure of the tree and its fruit.

p153.s4.b2.q: And as you now choose, so shall you eventually be.

p153.s4.b3: When asked for a predetermined sign, Jesus answered that no sign would be given beyond what they already had and what they would see when the Son of Man departed. The apostles, amazed and somewhat terror-stricken at this militant manner they had never seen in the Master, led him home in silence to Bethsaida.
p153.s5.h: V. The Saturday Evening — The Sifting and the Pledge of Loyalty
p153.s5.b0: The apostles had seen their hopes dashed many times before, but no disappointment had ever equaled this one. Near midnight Joab reported that about one third of the evangelists had deserted, and others brought word of a general revulsion of feeling toward the Master. Yet of the twelve women gathered at Peter’s house, not one deserted.

p153.s5.b2: A little after midnight Jesus stood before about thirty of them and told them this sifting was unavoidable; why grieve when a new day was dawning? He said he had known from the beginning that the halfhearted believers would fall out by the way, and he urged each of them to look to his own faith, for one of them stood in grave danger.

p153.s5.b3.q: it is the spirit that quickens; the flesh and all that pertains thereto is of little profit.

p153.s5.b4: When Jesus asked whether they too would desert, Peter answered that though they were sad and perplexed they would never forsake him, for he had taught them the words of eternal life. All of them nodded their approval of that pledge, and Jesus told them to go to their rest, for active days were just ahead.
p153.s6.b0: Paper 153 records the day when success measured in numbers collapsed, yet it is not a record of failure but of sifting. Jesus offered the bread that gives life to the soul instead of bread that fills the belly, and he asked for purity of heart instead of purity of hands. Faced with that demand, people either left or stayed, and the choice of those who stayed was the fruit of many small choices made over time.

p153.s6.b2: In the next paper, Paper 154, “Last Days at Capernaum,” Jesus and the apostles prepare to leave Capernaum under mounting pressure from Herod and the Sanhedrin.
p154.lead: Three weeks from the closing of the synagogues to Herod’s order of arrest: a painful misunderstanding with his family, and the start of a final year with nowhere to lay his head.

p154.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p154.s0.h: Introduction — The Council at Tiberias and Herod’s Hesitation
p154.s0.b0: On that Saturday night of the Capernaum crisis, while Jesus was comforting his disciples, special commissioners of the Sanhedrin were at Tiberias urging Herod Antipas to arrest him. This paper covers the three weeks or so from that night to the morning of May 22, when Jesus fled by boat. At its center is the way Jesus treated his followers and his family as the pressure closed in.
p154.s0.b1: At first Herod refused to deal with Jesus as a political offender, and the text gives several reasons why. When the Jews threatened to report to Caesar that he was shielding a traitor, he ordered them out of his council chamber, and matters rested there for a week.

head: Why Herod refused to arrest him
What the text says
rows: Accurate reports
His advisers had reported that Jesus rejected the offer of kingship
Chuza’s testimony

Fear of John the Baptist

p154.s1.h: I. A Week of Counsel — Healthy Growth from the Lowest Ebb
p154.s1.b0: From May 1 to May 7 Jesus held counsel at the Zebedee house, morning, afternoon, and evening, with the tried and trusted disciples only. About one hundred had the moral courage to brave the opposition of the Pharisees and openly follow him. On Friday of that week the Capernaum synagogue was closed to Jesus and his followers, and Jairus resigned as chief ruler and openly took his stand with Jesus.
p154.s1.b1: Fewer than one hundred and fifty gathered at the last seaside meeting on May 7. The text calls this night the lowest ebb of popular regard, yet it adds that from then on a slower but healthier growth of favorable sentiment began. The compromising stage, in which material and spiritual ideas of the kingdom had been mixed together, now came to an end.

p154.s1.b2.q: a new following was built up which was better grounded in spiritual faith and true religious experience.

p154.s2.h: II. A Week of Rest — Caring for the Sick Without a Miracle
p154.s2.b0: On May 8 the Sanhedrin passed a decree closing every synagogue in Palestine to Jesus and his followers. Since each synagogue had always been an independent congregation, this was an unprecedented usurpation of authority, and five members of the Sanhedrin resigned. Only the synagogue at Hebron refused, not out of sympathy with Jesus but to defend congregational autonomy; shortly afterward it was destroyed by fire.
p154.s2.b1: That same day Jesus declared a week’s holiday for his disciples. He urged them to go home or to their friends, rest their troubled souls, and encourage their loved ones. There was no public teaching that week; Jesus visited families about the seaside and went fishing with David Zebedee.

p154.s2.b2.q: Go to your several places to play or fish while you pray for the extension of the kingdom.

p154.s2.b3: During that week Nathaniel and James Zebedee were ill for three days with a painful digestive disturbance. On the third night Jesus sent Salome to rest and nursed them himself. He could have healed them instantly, but he did not. The text explains that never once in his life in the flesh did Jesus perform any supernatural ministry for his earth family or his immediate followers, and it gives the reason.

p154.s2.b4.q: The animal nature and the lower forms of will creatures do not progress favorably in environmental ease.

p154.s2.b5: Difficulties are not accidents to be avoided but part of the experience training provided for the growth of the soul. Problem situations, joined with the stimulus of effort, call forth the activities of mind, soul, and spirit. For the reader who asks in the midst of suffering why God does not rescue at once, this passage shows that the love that stays and cares may differ from the power that removes by miracle.
p154.s3.h: III–IV. The Second Tiberias Conference; Saturday Night in Capernaum
p154.s3.b0: At the second Tiberias conference on May 16, the Jewish leaders reported that practically every synagogue had been closed. Herod at first refused again, but then gave way: if the Roman ruler agreed, the Sanhedrin could take Jesus to Jerusalem for trial. When word of that agreement came on the night of May 21, he signed the decree authorizing the arrest just before midnight, yielding to pressure though he knew well that Jesus could not expect a fair trial in Jerusalem.

p154.s3.b2: That same Saturday night fifty leading citizens of Capernaum debated past midnight over the question “⟦Q 154:4.1⟧What shall we do with Jesus?⟦/Q⟧” but could reach no agreement. Apart from a few who thought he might be the Messiah or a prophet, the meeting split into four nearly equal groups.

p154.s3.b4: His enemies argued that his teachings were impractical and that everything would go to pieces if everybody tried to live by them. The narrator grants that many well-meaning people say much the same today, but points out that they forget an important fact: a much better civilization could have been built on Jesus’ teachings, and sometime will be.

p154.s3.b5.q: This world has never seriously tried to carry out the teachings of Jesus on a large scale

p154.s4.h: V. The Eventful Sunday Morning — Parting Instructions
p154.s4.b0: Before dawn on May 22 one of David’s messengers brought word that Herod had authorized the arrest. David Zebedee called an emergency council for seven o’clock, and Jesus gave farewell instructions to the disciples who were soon to be scattered. He told them to seek God’s guidance and carry on the work of the kingdom regardless of consequences.

Jesus’ instructions
rows: All the disciples
Seek God for guidance and carry on the work regardless of consequences
The evangelists

The twelve apostles

The twelve women

David Zebedee

p154.s4.b2: David assured him that the messengers would never lose contact, and that whatever happened to him, he had already appointed leaders to succeed him. At about half past seven Jesus began his parting address to nearly one hundred believers; though the occasion was solemn, he was unusually cheerful, once more like his normal self.

p154.s4.b3.q: I am neither a teacher nor a preacher, but it is in my heart to do this, and none can stop me.

p154.s5.h: VI. Jesus’ Family Arrives — A Meeting That Missed
p154.s5.b0: About eight o’clock Mary, James, Joseph, Jude, and Ruth arrived at the Zebedee house. The night before, the Pharisees had worked to persuade Mary that Jesus was beside himself and that she and her sons should take him home. While Jesus was popular, the family had let matters drift; now that the people had turned against him, they felt keenly the supposed disgrace, and they feared for their own safety.

head: Family member
Attitude toward Jesus
rows: Ruth
Believed wholeheartedly and continuously in the divinity of his mission; opposed the plan to dissuade him
Jude, James, and Joseph
Kept much of their faith, but let pride cloud their better judgment
Mary
Torn between love and fear, mother love and family pride; could never quite forget Gabriel’s visit

p154.s5.b2: When Peter whispered that his mother and brothers were outside, Jesus did not break off his address but sent word that they should have no fear for him. Then, stretching out his hands toward the disciples in the room, he said that those who do the Father’s will are his family. When Mary heard this, she collapsed.

p154.s5.b3.q: For whosoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, the same is my mother, my brother, and my sister.

p154.s5.b4: The text explains the circumstances carefully so that we do not read the scene as coldness. Jesus did not want their first meeting after so long a separation to become a public affair in the middle of his discourse, and he meant to see them once he had finished. But the news that the arresting officers were coming, and a commotion at the rear entrance, sent the company hurrying out the front to the boat, and he never saw his family waiting on the back porch.
p154.s5.b5: While Mary was recovering in the garden, a woman in the room cried out that the womb that bore him was blessed. Jesus honored the courage to hear and obey the word above the honor of kinship. His family thought he had lost interest in them, little realizing that it was they who had failed to understand him.

p154.s5.b6.q: No, rather is the one blessed who hears the word of God and dares to obey it.

p154.s5.b7: Jesus knew that people may be easily moved by a sermon and readily respond to logic, yet find it far harder to break with their past. So he did not reproach his family’s misunderstanding but accepted it as something that would take time. Years later, after the resurrection, when James joined the early movement, he suffered immeasurably for having missed that earlier association.

p154.s5.b8.q: Jesus did not forsake his earth family to do his Father’s work—they forsook him.

p154.s5.b9.q: It is forever true that all who may think they are misunderstood or not appreciated have in Jesus a sympathizing friend and an understanding counselor.

p154.s5.b10: As he stepped into the boat, Jesus asked David to tell his mother and brothers that he appreciated their coming and had intended to see them. He left them the counsel to seek a knowledge of God’s will and the grace and courage to do it. For anyone who feels the pain of a family whose path of faith has parted from his or her own, this section offers deep comfort.
p154.s6.h: VII. The Hasty Flight — Days with Nowhere to Lay His Head
p154.s6.b0: At about half past eight Jesus, with the twelve apostles and twelve evangelists, rowed for the eastern shore. A smaller boat carrying six of David’s messengers followed to keep up communication. Jesus was never again to make his home at the Zebedee house, so long the headquarters of the kingdom.
p154.s6.b1: For the rest of his earth life the Master had no settled abode. The party left their boat with friends near Kheresa and stayed for a time in the domains of Philip, beginning the eventful wanderings that would take them by way of Caesarea-Philippi to the coast of Phoenicia.
p154.s6.b2: The Jerusalem officers arrived only after the boats had gone and spent nearly a week searching vainly around Capernaum. Jesus’ family passed that week in confusion, and found peace only on Thursday afternoon, when Ruth learned from David that her brother was safe and making his way toward the Phoenician coast.
p154.s7.b0: Paper 154 portrays a time when power was closing in from outside and even his own family misunderstood him. Through it all Jesus ordered rest, nursed his sick apostles with his own hands, and was cheerful at the moment of parting. The text’s observation that a better-grounded fellowship of faith began to grow from the lowest ebb of numbers is a hope for any community passing through a season of decline.

Play or fish while you pray (154:2.2)

p154.s7.b2: In the next paper, Paper 155, “Fleeing Through Northern Galilee,” Jesus and his company wander north through the domains of Philip while he continues his teaching on the true nature of religion.
p155.lead: Two discourses on religion given on the road of flight: the heart of this paper is the contrast between the religion of the mind, resting on tradition’s authority, and the religion of the spirit, grounded in personal experience.

p155.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p155.s0.h: Introduction — The Road of Flight Becomes a School
p155.s0.b0: After leaving Capernaum, Jesus and the twenty-four landed near Kheresa and spent their first night in a park south of Bethsaida-Julias. That night Jesus discussed with them their projected tour through Batanea and northern Galilee to the Phoenician coast. This paper follows the first three weeks of that journey, centering on the two discourses on religion he gave near Luz.
p155.s0.b1: Outwardly it was a journey of men being hunted, yet the text does not write this period as a record of failure. They made few converts, but the apostles and evangelists learned much from their daily conversations with the Master. Where outward results had disappeared, the essence of religion came up for question once again.
p155.s1.h: I. Why Do the Heathen Rage? — A Kingdom of Love
p155.s1.b0: Jesus quoted the psalm in which the rulers take counsel against the Lord and his anointed, and said that its words were being fulfilled before their eyes. But the rest of the Psalmist’s picture—the wrathful Son—would not be fulfilled, for the Psalmist had held mistaken ideas about the Son of Man and his mission.

p155.s1.b1.q: My kingdom is founded on love, proclaimed in mercy, and established by unselfish service.

head: The Psalmist’s exhortation
Jesus’ exhortation
rows: Serve the Lord with fear
Enter by faith into the exalted privileges of divine sonship
Rejoice with trembling
Rejoice with assurance
Kiss the Son, lest he be angry and you perish
Anger and wrath are no part of establishing the kingdom
Break the heathen with a rod of iron
Receive these ignorant brethren with open arms of mercy and affection

p155.s1.b3: Jesus even pointed out something the disciples could learn from their enemies. Their outlook was narrow, but for that very reason they concentrated all their energies on their goal. The disciples, by contrast, were caught up in regretting the past, whining over the present, and vainly hoping for the future.

p155.s1.b4.q: Why do the heathen rage? Because they know not the truth. Why do you languish in futile yearning? Because you obey not the truth.

p155.s1.b5: He also warned against narrowness and overspecialization. The Greeks with science but no religion and the Jews with religion but no science are both left with fragments of truth. His saying that people will seek us out if we live a truth-coordinated life means that we should first test the success of our witness in our own lives.

p155.s1.b6.q: The measure wherewith truth seekers are drawn to you represents the measure of your truth endowment, your righteousness.

p155.s2.h: II–III. Chorazin and Caesarea-Philippi — A Baptism of Adversity
p155.s2.b0: Peter and the twelve evangelists spent two weeks in Chorazin, while Jesus and the eleven apostles spent two weeks at Caesarea-Philippi. No city in all Galilee yielded so few souls as Chorazin, and for the evangelists those two weeks were the hardest and most unproductive time of their careers. Yet that very lack made each of them take stock more honestly of his own soul’s progress.

head: Company

rows: Peter and the twelve evangelists

Jesus and the eleven apostles
Caesarea-Philippi, two weeks from May 24

Wednesday, June 8
Learned from the parable of the sower the meaning of apparent failure

p155.s2.b2: What the apostles learned at Caesarea prepared them for the discourses later in the paper. When truth is crystallized into a creed, it becomes a boundary line of self-righteousness instead of a signpost, and it fossilizes. Many souls are best led to love the unseen God by first learning to love the brethren they can see. And a faith resting only on material longings will crumble as knowledge of nature grows, whereas a spiritual religion can never be disturbed by the progress of physical science.

p155.s2.b3.q: true religion was man’s heartfelt loyalty to his highest and truest convictions.

p155.s2.b4.q: His whole earth life was consistently devoted to the mission of thawing out the frozen forms of religion into the liquid liberties of enlightened sonship.

p155.s3.h: IV–V. On the Way to Phoenicia; The Discourse on True Religion
p155.s3.b0: As they stopped for lunch in the shade of a rock ledge near Luz, Peter asked why they were fleeing instead of confronting their enemies, and Thomas asked what the real difference was between their religion and that of the Jerusalem leaders. Jesus said it would help them all more if he answered Thomas’s question. The discourse that followed is given in summary and restated in modern phraseology.

head: Three forms of religious devotion
Character
Basis
rows: Primitive religion
Fear of mysterious energies and worship of superior forces — the religion of the physical nature, the religion of fear
A seminatural and instinctive urge
The religion of civilization
Advancing religious concepts and practices — the religion of the mind, intellectual theology
The authority of established religious tradition
True religion — the religion of revelation
Revelation of supernatural values, a glimpse of the Father’s goodness and beauty — the religion of the spirit
Demonstrated in human experience

p155.s3.b2: Jesus refused to belittle the primitive forms, though he deplored how much of them persisted even in the religions of the more intelligent races. The religion of authority offers a ready refuge to a soul harassed by fear and uncertainty, and asks in return only passive intellectual assent. But those who cast their lot in that way give up the supreme adventure of human existence: man seeking God, for himself and as himself, and finding him.

p155.s3.b3.q: The religion of the spirit means effort, struggle, conflict, faith, determination, love, loyalty, and progress.

p155.s3.b4: Jesus described the religion of the Jerusalem leaders as an established system of intellectual beliefs built from many doctrines—a religion of authority. The new religion they were about to proclaim would appeal instead to the Father’s spirit dwelling in the mind of man, and would draw its authority from the fruits that appear in the personal experience of those who accept its truths. The question of where religious authority comes from runs through the whole discourse.
p155.s3.b5: Calling each of the twenty-four by name, Jesus asked which of them would choose the easy path of a fossilized religion over the way of the spirit with its persecutions. All of them rose to answer, but he raised his hand and stopped them. Because this was one of the few emotional appeals he ever made, he told them to find an unemotional answer before the Father.

p155.s3.b6.q: Go now apart by yourselves, each man alone with the Father

p155.s3.b7: When they reassembled, Jesus only told them to pray that their emotions would be transformed into higher loyalties and experiences of the spirit. As they walked on, the talk among them ripened, and at about three o’clock Peter begged him to say more. His way of giving the emotional moment time to mature, rather than turning it at once into a decision, was itself a lesson.
p155.s4.h: VI. The Second Discourse on Religion — Find God for Yourself
p155.s4.b0: At Peter’s request Jesus taught again in the shade of a hillside. The Father did not stop speaking words of truth when the old prophets ended their utterances, he said; so do not call divine what is wholly human, and do not fail to discern truth that comes from outside the traditional channels. He urged them not merely to quote the prophets but to become living prophets themselves.

p155.s4.b1.q: aspire to become living prophets of the Most High and spiritual heroes of the coming kingdom.

p155.s4.b2: He called them to be born again, born of the spirit. That means coming out of the darkness of authority and the lethargy of tradition to discover God for oneself, in oneself, as a fact of one’s own experience. To move from a racial faith inherited to a personal faith achieved by actual experience—that is the progress this passage describes.
p155.s4.b3: Jesus rebuked the false teachers who drag hungry souls back into the distant past and leave them there. Such people are frightened by every new discovery and discomfited by every new revelation. The prophet who knew perfect peace with his mind stayed on God was not someone who talked about God but someone who had found him.

head: Religion of the mind (authority)
Religion of the spirit (experience)
rows: Upheld by ecclesiastical authority
Wholly based on human experience
Ties you hopelessly to the past
Progressive revelation, ever beckoning toward higher achievement

Progressively draws men together in sympathetic understanding
Requires uniformity of belief
Requires only unity of experience, allowing diversity of belief
Crystallizes into lifeless creeds
Grows into loving service and merciful ministration

p155.s4.b5: Yet Jesus warned them not to look down on Israel. From Moses to Amos and Hosea, their persistent search had prepared the way for the greater revelation of the Father. To choose the religion of the spirit is not to despise tradition but to go beyond it.
p155.s4.b6: There is only one adventure more thrilling than discovering God’s will, and that is honestly trying to do it. That will can be done in any occupation, and all things are sacred in the lives of those who are spirit led. Jesus commended not the mental immaturity of a child but the spiritual simplicity of an easy-believing, fully trusting little one.

p155.s4.b7.q: Some callings are not holy and others secular.

p155.s4.b8.q: It is not so important that you should know about the fact of God as that you should increasingly grow in the ability to feel the presence of God.

p155.s4.b9: Jesus told them not to try to prove to others that they had found God; such proof cannot be produced consciously. There are, however, two positive demonstrations that a person knows God.

head: Two demonstrations of knowing God
What they are
rows: First
The fruits of the spirit of God showing forth in daily routine life
Second
A whole life plan that risks everything one is and has on the adventure of survival, in the hope of finding the God of eternity

p155.s4.b11.q: Now, mistake not, my Father will ever respond to the faintest flicker of faith.

p155.s4.b12: The Father honors even the superstitious emotions of primitive man and the feeble attempts of fearful souls whose faith never goes beyond intellectual assent to authority. But those called out of darkness into light are expected to believe with a whole heart—body, mind, and spirit. Religion must not be a theological shelter to flee into, but an experience that testifies that God has found us and lifted us up.
p155.s5.b0: Paper 155 offers one of the clearest statements in The Urantia Book of what religion is. Jesus calls us to choose the adventure that experience demands over the security that authority provides, yet he asks us to make that choice not in the heat of emotion but in quiet decision before the Father. His teaching that we should seek unity of spirit feeling rather than uniformity of belief is especially practical for readers today who live among many different convictions.

head: Practice
The teaching behind it
rows: Live a truth-coordinated life before trying to persuade others
The measure of attraction is the measure of righteousness (155:1.5)

The baptism of adversity at Chorazin (155:2.2)
Make important decisions alone before the Father
Find the unemotional answer (155:5.14)
Treat daily work as a place to do God’s will
No callings are holy and others secular (155:6.11)
Grow in the ability to feel God’s presence more than in knowing doctrine
Feeling the presence matters more (155:6.12)
Seek unity of spirit with those of different beliefs
Full allowance for diversity of belief (155:6.9)

p155.s5.b2: In the next paper, Paper 156, “The Sojourn at Tyre and Sidon,” the company stays on the Phoenician coast and continues teaching among the gentiles.
p156.lead: About six weeks among the gentiles of Phoenicia: Norana’s persistent faith, the parables of the white lily and the rotten beam, and the way to overcome temptation.

p156.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p156.s0.h: Introduction — A Door Opened Where He Went to Rest
p156.s0.b0: On June 10 Jesus and his company reached the environs of Sidon and stayed at the home of Karuska, a well-to-do woman who had once been a patient in the Bethsaida hospital. They spent about six weeks in Phoenicia—in Sidon, the coast cities, and Tyre. Jesus had come there to rest, yet at the very time the doors had closed in Galilee, the work among the gentiles proved remarkably fruitful.
p156.s0.b1: The first Sabbath was one of great quiet. The apostles and evangelists meditated on the discourses on religion they had heard along the way, but none of them fully grasped their meaning. This paper shows how that teaching came alive in actual ministry among the gentiles.
p156.s1.h: I. The Syrian Woman — The Faith of a Believing Dog
p156.s1.b0: Karuska’s servant told a neighbor, a Syrian woman named Norana, that Jesus was lodging there. Norana came with her daughter, about twelve years old, who suffered from convulsions and a grievous nervous disorder; she believed the child was possessed by an unclean spirit. One apostle after another tried to send her away because the Master was resting, but she would not give up.

What he said
Norana’s reply

She would wait right there until he had finished his rest
Peter
He is weary with teaching and healing and came here to rest
She would not depart until she had seen the Master
Thomas
Tried to send her away

Simon Zelotes
The children’s bread should not be cast to the dogs
Even the dogs may have the crumbs that fall from the children’s table

p156.s1.b2.q: I am only a dog in the eyes of the Jews, but as concerns your Master, I am a believing dog.

p156.s1.b3: Jesus, who had heard everything through an open window, came out and told her that her faith was great indeed, and the girl was well from that hour. The scene sets the disciples’ prejudice sharply against the faith of a gentile woman. The next day Jesus said that the Father’s kingdom would be taken by the gentiles if the children of Abraham did not show faith enough to enter it.

p156.s1.b4.q: O woman, great is your faith

p156.s1.b5: The text adds that what touched the Master’s heart was not only Norana’s persistent faith but also her sense of humor. Her way of turning a cutting remark aside with good-humored wit shows a humble strength that does not lose its purpose even when insulted.
p156.s2.h: II. Teaching in Sidon — A Life on the Bridge
p156.s2.b0: On entering Sidon, many in the company crossed a bridge for the first time in their lives, and Jesus used it to sum up the nature of this world. He then stayed at the home of Justa and her mother Bernice, teaching the twenty-four each morning, while they preached in Sidon in the afternoons and evenings.

p156.s2.b1.q: This world is only a bridge; you may pass over it, but you should not think to build a dwelling place upon it.

p156.s2.b2: These Greek-speaking gentile believers in many ways appreciated the teachings more fully than the Jews. They came to know not only that Jesus was like God but also that God was like Jesus, and they grasped that there is no favoritism with the Universal Father and that the universe is ever law-abiding and dependable.

p156.s2.b3.q: All down through the ages men have not been unable to comprehend Jesus; they have been afraid to.

p156.s2.b4: Jesus made it clear that he had not left Galilee for lack of courage, but because the time had not yet come for an open clash with established religion. His theme at Sidon was spiritual progression. One cannot stand still but must go forward or retrogress; we must not only cease to do evil but learn to do well, and once our sins are confessed, we must refuse to harbor even the feelings of guilt.

p156.s2.b5.q: My people take themselves too seriously

p156.s2.b6: Jesus greatly enjoyed the keen humor of these gentiles, and said that the burdensome religion of the Pharisees could never have arisen among a people with a sense of humor. That earnest faith and a light touch toward oneself can go together is a valuable lesson for believers today.
p156.s3.h: III–IV. The Journey up the Coast; At Tyre
p156.s3.b0: Using Sidon as their base, the company taught in the coast cities to the north and as far south as Tyre. The apostles and evangelists were greatly surprised by the eagerness of these gentiles and the readiness with which they believed. The text explains that these people were in reality mainly descended from the earlier Canaanite tribes.

p156.s3.b2: The polyglot population of Tyre heard them gladly, and many were baptized. Interest ran so high that the doors of the Melkarth temple were opened to Jesus, and in later years a Christian church was built on that very site. Many of the makers of Tyrian purple believed, and when they migrated to the ends of the earth in search of new shellfish beds, they carried the gospel of the kingdom with them.
p156.s4.h: V. Jesus’ Teaching at Tyre — The White Lily, the Beam, and Temptation
p156.s4.b0: In his address of July 20 Jesus first told the story of the white lily: though its roots are grounded in the dark muck below, it rears its pure head high into the sunshine.

p156.s4.b1.q: mortal man, while he has his roots of origin and being in the animal soil of human nature, can by faith raise his spiritual nature up into the sunlight of heavenly truth and actually bear the noble fruits of the spirit.

p156.s4.b2: In the same sermon he told his first and only parable about carpentry. Do not be the foolish carpenter who spends all his labor squaring and smoothing a worm-eaten beam, only to find it unfit for the foundation. The intellectual and moral foundations of character must be sound enough to support the superstructure of the spiritual nature. Mind and morals are the soil; the soul is the living growth that springs from it.
p156.s4.b3: That evening Nathaniel asked why they should pray not to be led into temptation if God never does such a thing. Jesus answered that their forefathers, seeing God’s hand in everything, had attributed even temptation to him, but that men are usually led into temptation by their own selfishness and the impulses of their animal natures. He then contrasted two ways of meeting temptation.

Result

Deliverance through spiritual transformation — the old forgotten in love for the new

p156.s4.b5.q: There is mighty power in the expulsive energy of a new and sincere spiritual affection.

p156.s4.b6: The questions and answers that went on long into the night are given restated in modern phraseology. Like short proverbs, they serve as a mirror of a believer’s character. Human nature may tend toward evil, but it is not inherently sinful, and spiritual destiny is conditioned only by spiritual longings and purposes.

p156.s4.b7.q: The mistakes which you fail to forget in time will be forgotten in eternity.

What the text names

The soul’s spiritual capacity
Faith in truth and love for man
Strength of character
Resisting grudges and withstanding brooding in deep sorrow

p156.s4.b9.q: Love is never self-seeking, and it cannot be self-bestowed.

p156.s4.b10.q: Defeat is the true mirror in which you may honestly view your real self.

p156.s4.b11.q: Tact is the fulcrum of social leverage, and tolerance is the earmark of a great soul.

p156.s4.b12: These sayings also address the believer’s inner stability. Believers must learn to step aside from the rush of life and renew the soul in worshipful communion. God-knowing people are not discouraged by misfortune nor depressed by material upheavals, and they endure unavoidable suffering without complaint. Difficulty only whets the ardor of the truth lover.

p156.s4.b13.q: Every day a true believer lives, he finds it easier to do the right thing.

p156.s4.b14: These sayings do not confine faith to inner feeling. Self-respect cannot exceed love of one’s neighbor; we are to be citizens of heaven and useful citizens of earth; and we must seek no unearned recognition. The day before leaving Tyre, Jesus sent the twelve evangelists home by another route, and they were never again so intimately associated with him.
p156.s5.h: VI. The Return from Phoenicia — The Battle Lines Drawn
p156.s5.b0: Jesus and the twelve went by way of Ptolemais, Jotapata, Ramah, and Zebulun to Gennesaret, where they met David Zebedee. They then crossed to near Kheresa and, in the park where the five thousand had been fed, held three days of conferences with about fifty men and women—the remnant of the once numerous believers of Capernaum.

In what way

p156.s5.b2: So it was that about the first of August, A.D. 29, Jesus began to reorganize his scattered and depleted forces. The text closes by observing that, as they prepared to proclaim the religion of the spirit of the living God, the issues of battle were now clearly drawn.
p156.s6.b0: Paper 156 shows that the place to which we are driven can become the place where we bear fruit. The humble and good-humored faith of a gentile woman, the view of this world as a bridge, and the white lily blooming from the muck all point in the same direction. And the sayings at Tyre remind us that faith must become a practical skill for dealing with failure, grudges, and temptation.

p157.lead: A missed family visit, the temple tax, the signs of the times, and Peter’s confession at Caesarea-Philippi: the paper in which the fourth stage of Jesus’ life begins.

p157.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p157.s0.h: Introduction — The Family He Could Not Meet
p157.s0.b0: In August of A.D. 29, before taking the twelve on a short sojourn to Caesarea-Philippi, Jesus arranged to meet his family at the Zebedee boatshop in Capernaum. David Zebedee and Jesus’ brother Jude had arranged for Mary and the whole family to come, but a group of Pharisees from Jerusalem got wind of it and installed themselves in Mary’s home. The family could not leave the house, and when Jesus heard of it, he gave up the visit.
p157.s0.b1: The text records quietly that this happened through no fault of either side. It is common in life for two parties with good intentions to miss each other because of circumstances beyond them. The paper begins with such a missed meeting and goes on to record the decisive days in which it finally became clear to the apostles who Jesus was.
p157.s1.h: I. The Temple-Tax Collector — The Wisdom of Giving No Offense
p157.s1.b0: As Jesus and his companions waited by the lake, a temple-tax collector came up and asked Peter whether the Master did not pay the temple tax. Peter was inclined to be indignant at the idea of supporting the religious work of their enemies, but sensing a plan to trap them into refusing the half shekel, he promised at once to pay. The money, however, was with Judas on the other side of the lake.

p157.s1.b1.q: Let us give these men no occasion for offense at our attitude.

p157.s1.b2: Jesus told Peter to catch some fish, sell them, and pay the tax for all three of them. David’s secret messenger, who had overheard, and a fisherman friend handed Peter several baskets of fish and added money to the sale, and so the tax was met. The text explains that Jesus’ half-humorous remark—“⟦Q 157:1.4⟧maybe you will catch the fish with the shekel in its mouth⟦/Q⟧”—later grew into a miracle story.

p157.s1.b4: The story shows Jesus’ practical wisdom in avoiding needless conflict where no principle is at stake. It also shows the honesty of keeping one’s word, and how ordinary cooperation can turn into a miracle as it is retold.
p157.s2.h: II. At Bethsaida-Julias — Discern the Times Rather Than Demand Signs
p157.s2.b0: On August 8 more than one hundred believers, evangelists, and members of the women’s corps gathered for a conference at Magadan Park, and Pharisees came too—now joined by some of the Sadducees. The hecklers demanded a sign of his authority, and Jesus asked how they could discern the face of the heavens yet fail to discern the signs of the times.

p157.s2.b1.q: To those who would know the truth, already has a sign been given

p157.s2.b2: At the evening conference they decided on a united mission throughout the Decapolis as soon as Jesus and the twelve returned from Caesarea-Philippi. Dismissing the company, Jesus warned them to beware the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees and to place their faith not in dead forms but in living experience.

p157.s2.b3.q: It is not the purpose of true religion merely to bring peace but rather to insure progress.

p157.s2.b4: This charge still holds for believers today. Respect for learning and tradition is valuable, but when it blinds the eyes and stops the ears, it becomes leaven. His counsel not to stifle feelings of love for a neighbor but to express them in intelligent ministry to that person’s real needs is a concrete guide for joining feeling to action.
p157.s3.h: III. Peter’s Confession — “Who Say You That I Am?”
p157.s3.b0: Early Tuesday morning the company set out for Caesarea-Philippi, with Mount Hermon in full view. Jesus wished to return to that mount of trial and triumph from his early ministry, hoping the apostles would gain new strength there for the trying times ahead. When they paused for lunch, he asked them for the first time a question about himself.

p157.s3.b2.q: You are the Deliverer, the Son of the living God.

p157.s3.b3: Peter sprang to his feet and spoke, and the other eleven rose with one accord. Jesus said this had been revealed to them by his Father, yet charged them to tell no one for the time being. That night the apostles slept little, sensing that a great event in their lives had taken place.
p157.s4.h: IV. The Talk about the Kingdom — The Rock of Spiritual Reality
p157.s4.b0: Since the baptism and Cana, the apostles had several times come close to accepting him as the Messiah, but each time some word or deed of Jesus had dashed their hopes, and they had long been in turmoil. The next day in Celsus’ garden the two Simons labored to bring their brethren to accept Jesus not only as the Messiah but as the divine Son of God. When the twelve rose to greet him, Jesus smiled and waved them to their seats, and they never again showed him such an outward mark of respect.
p157.s4.b1: Jesus asked whether, a full day later, they still held to their decision, and Peter confessed again. Jesus said that this belief was not human knowledge but a revelation of the Father’s spirit, and he declared that upon it he would build the brotherhood of the kingdom of heaven.

p157.s4.b2.q: Upon this rock of spiritual reality will I build the living temple of spiritual fellowship in the eternal realities of my Father’s kingdom.

p157.s4.b3: He left spiritual guidance to the Father’s spirit, and to the apostles and their successors he delivered the keys of the outward kingdom—authority over the social and economic affairs of the fellowship of believers. The distinction matters: the authority to manage a community and the spirit’s guidance of each soul belong to different levels. The text adds that those who become self-conscious sons of God are the human stones of this living temple.
p157.s4.b4: On this day Jesus began to believe in the faith of his apostles—all but one. He foresaw that even after the apparent wreckage of their hopes, their faith would go on to enlighten the world in a new light.
p157.s5.h: V. The New Concept — Son of Man and Son of God
p157.s5.b0: What was new in Peter’s confession was the clear recognition of Jesus’ divinity. The Messiah the Jews awaited was to be the “anointed one,” not one who sprang from divinity. The second confession emphasized his combined nature as Son of Man and Son of God, and it was on this truth that Jesus said he would build the kingdom.

head: Jesus’ approach

Third — to announce his divinity openly

p157.s5.b2: Jesus decided to stop trying to convince them that he was not the Messiah. Instead he boldly revealed what he is and simply ignored their insistence on regarding him as the Messiah. It is an attitude of showing the truth plainly and leaving understanding to time, rather than endlessly correcting another’s misunderstanding.
p157.s6.h: VI. The Next Afternoon — The Fourth Stage of His Life
p157.s6.b0: After his popularity collapsed, the treasury was empty, but David Zebedee had foreseen this and had his messengers collect funds, which arrived in time to carry them until the Decapolis tour. Matthew, too, arranged for the money from the sale of his last property to go anonymously to Judas. At this point the apostles had confessed Jesus’ divinity, but they had no adequate idea of what it meant.
p157.s6.b1: Yet from this time a new note appeared in the Master’s message. His one ideal of living became the revelation of the Father, and his teaching centered on presenting to his universe that supreme wisdom which can only be comprehended by living it. The passage reminds us that truth shown in a life goes deeper than truth explained in words.

p157.s6.b2.q: He came that we all might have life and have it more abundantly.

p157.s6.b4: The text says that Jesus exemplified in his own life what he taught: not an incessant struggle between soul and body, but the growth of the spiritual nature through living progress. His teaching that the spirit is easy victor over both and reconciles much of the warfare between intellect and instinct offers another way to those worn out from fighting themselves.

p157.s6.b5.q: I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.

p157.s6.b6: That day in the garden Jesus told them to assume the obligations of sonship and follow him, that he had come to minister, that before Abraham was, he is, and that he and the Father are one. When he asked whether they could believe this even though his kingdom was not of this world and he had nowhere to lay his head, the apostles listened in stunned silence.

p157.s6.b7.q: the Father and I are one. He who has seen me has seen the Father.

p157.s7.h: VII. Andrew’s Conference — The Shadow of Judas
p157.s7.b0: That evening Andrew held searching talks with each of his brethren, finding all of them heartening except Judas Iscariot. Worried by Judas’s attitude, he went to Jesus late that night, but Jesus only said there was nothing more they could do; Andrew should go on placing the utmost confidence in Judas and say nothing to the others.

p157.s7.b2: The other apostles went through the same trials, but they loved Jesus. Judas’s great mistake was that whenever Jesus sent them off alone to pray, instead of communing with the spiritual forces of the universe, he indulged in thoughts of fear and nursed doubts and feelings of revenge. The passage shows that, faced with the same trials, what separates people is what they fill their hours alone with.
p157.s7.b3: On the morning of Friday, August 12, Jesus told the apostles to prepare for a journey to the mountain. He was beginning the fourth phase of his ministry as the Son of God, and as at his baptism, he wanted some of them present as witnesses to hear his authority for it.
p157.s8.b0: Paper 157 marks the turning point at which understanding of Jesus moves from “a prophet” to “⟦Q 157:4.5⟧the Son of God.⟦/Q⟧” Yet that confession begins not as knowledge in the head but as a revelation from the Father’s spirit, and what is built upon it is not an institution but a living temple of spiritual fellowship. The paper’s deepest invitation is that each reader may become a stone in that temple.

p158.lead: The transfiguration on Mount Hermon, the healing of the epileptic boy, and Peter’s protest with its sharp rebuke: Jesus enters the final phase of his life as the Son of God.

p158.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p158.s0.h: Introduction — At the Foot of Mount Hermon
p158.s0.b0: Near sundown on August 12, A.D. 29, Jesus and the apostles reached the foot of Mount Hermon, close to the place where the lad Tiglath had once waited while the Master went up the mountain alone and technically terminated the Lucifer rebellion. They stayed there two days in spiritual preparation for what was to follow.
p158.s0.b1: Jesus wished all his apostles could share the experience on the mountain, but none of them had reached the spiritual level that would justify exposure to the visitation of celestial beings. So he took only Peter, James, and John, who usually accompanied him on such special vigils. This paper portrays, within a single week, glory on the mountain, failure below it, and the first clear foretelling of his death.
p158.s1.h: I. The Transfiguration — The Choice to Decline Universe Authority
p158.s1.b0: On Monday, August 15, six days after Peter’s confession, Jesus climbed the mountain with the three apostles. The text notes the significance that this event took place in the lands of the gentiles, on a gentile mountain. As a boy he had climbed the hill near his home and dreamed of the battles of empires; now he climbed a mountain to receive the endowment for the closing scenes of his bestowal.
p158.s1.b1: That day Jesus could have relinquished the struggle and returned to his rule of the universe. But he chose not only to meet the requirements of the Eternal Son but also to fulfill the last and full measure of his Paradise Father’s present will. The three apostles watched him decline to be invested with full universe authority, and saw him left alone when the celestial messengers departed.
p158.s1.b2: At about three in the afternoon Jesus went apart for a long conference with Gabriel and the Father Melchizedek, returning about six o’clock to reassure his anxious apostles. That night the three, who had fallen asleep, were awakened by a crackling sound and saw Jesus talking with two brilliant beings clothed in light. Peter mistakenly took them for Moses and Elijah; in reality they were Gabriel and the Father Melchizedek.

p158.s1.b3.q: I now declare that the Son of Man has chosen to go through his full life in your midst and as one of you.

p158.s1.b4: In his confusion Peter proposed building three tents. Then a silvery cloud overshadowed them, and they heard the same voice that had spoken at the baptism. Jesus touched them as they lay on their faces and told them not to be afraid.

p158.s1.b5.q: This is my beloved Son; give heed to him.

p158.s2.h: II. Coming down the Mountain — Elijah Has Already Come
p158.s2.b0: Halfway down the mountain Jesus told them to tell no one what they had seen until the Son of Man had risen from the dead. Having just seen his glory, the apostles were shocked to hear of death and resurrection. To steer away from the subject, Peter asked about the scribes’ saying that Elijah must come first, and Jesus answered that Elijah had already come. The three realized that he meant John the Baptist.
p158.s2.b1: He enjoined silence so as not to foster their mistaken idea of a wonder-working Messiah. Jesus told them that since they would not receive him as the Son of Man, he had consented to be received according to their settled determination. But he warned them that this choice would carry a cost.

p158.s2.b2.q: but the training which I have given you should suffice to bring you triumphantly through even these sorrows of your own choosing.

p158.s2.b3: The text makes clear that the three were not chosen because they were better prepared or more fit. None of the twelve was spiritually qualified; these three were simply the ones assigned to accompany him in times of solitary communion. That privilege is not proof of superiority is a lesson worth keeping in any community today.
p158.s3.h: III. Meaning of the Transfiguration — Three Testimonies
p158.s3.b0: What the three apostles saw was only a fleeting glimpse of a celestial pageant that took place that day on Mount Hermon. The text explains the transfiguration as the occasion of divine acknowledgment of the fullness of the bestowal.

p158.s3.b2: Jesus noted that the Father had not indicated the bestowal was finished, and he decided to pursue the mortal bestowal to its natural end. That was the meaning of the transfiguration for him. For the three apostles it marked the Master’s entrance upon the final phase of his earth career. It is striking how the same event carries different meanings depending on where one stands.
p158.s4.h: IV–V. The Epileptic Boy; Jesus Heals the Boy
p158.s4.b0: Below the mountain a very different scene was unfolding. James of Safed had spent nearly two weeks searching for Jesus with his only son, about fourteen years old, who was epileptic and possessed by a rebellious midwayer. When he arrived, the nine apostles were arguing about who should be greatest in the coming kingdom.
p158.s4.b1: Simon Zelotes and Judas Iscariot stepped forward, claiming that the keys of the kingdom had been given to them, and tried to cast out the demon, but the boy only had a more violent fit while the scribes mocked. Andrew tried again after prayer and also failed, and frankly confessed defeat. Meanwhile the three coming down the mountain were ecstatic, and the nine below lay sleepless in humiliation.
p158.s4.b2: When Jesus returned, the father knelt before him. Jesus rebuked them, saying that the works of faith do not come forth at the bidding of doubting unbelief, and he told the father to question not the Father’s power of love but only the sincerity and reach of his own faith.

p158.s4.b3.q: Lord, I believe. I pray you help my unbelief.

p158.s4.b4: Jesus raised the boy in accordance with the Father’s will and in honor of living faith. It was a true healing of a double affliction, physical and spiritual. The text adds that the twelve always alternated between exaltation and humiliation. The father’s confession, mingling faith and doubt, comforts us that an honestly seeking faith is accepted even without perfect certainty.
p158.s5.h: VI. In Celsus’ Garden — The Causes of Failure
p158.s5.b0: That evening Thomas asked Jesus to teach them about their defeat. Jesus pointed out that those who stayed behind, though instructed to pray, had failed to exercise their faith and had fallen back into the old tendency of seeking preferred places in the kingdom.

p158.s5.b1.q: Spiritual greatness consists in an understanding love that is Godlike and not in an enjoyment of the exercise of material power for the exaltation of self.

p158.s5.b3: Jesus said that spiritual work requires spiritual power, and that even where the potential is present, nothing can be done without the third and essential factor: the personal experience of living faith. He then told them again that the Son of Man would be put to death but would rise again. The apostles retired sorrowful, and remembered his words only after the resurrection.

p158.s5.b4.q: When can you be depended upon to adhere to the higher and spiritual realities of the kingdom regardless of the outward appearance of all material manifestations?

p158.s5.b5: This question is put to everyone who wants visible results to confirm faith. A faith that holds to spiritual realities even when prayer is not answered at once, or when good work ends in apparent failure—that is the maturity Jesus hoped for in his apostles.
p158.s6.h: VII. Peter’s Protest — When Love Becomes a Stumbling Block
p158.s6.b0: The next day Jesus avoided his critics by taking only the apostles along the Damascus road. When Andrew asked him to speak plainly rather than in parables, Jesus told them directly that he must be rejected in Jerusalem, be killed, and rise again. Peter impulsively laid his hand on the Master’s shoulder and declared that these things would never happen to him.
p158.s6.b1: Peter spoke out of love. But Jesus’ human nature recognized in that well-meant affection a subtle temptation to change his course of following the Father’s will to the end. So, with a rare flash of the eye, he rebuked him at once.

p158.s6.b2.q: Mind not the ways of men but rather the will of God.

p158.s6.b3: Jesus went on to tell them to disregard themselves, take up their responsibilities daily, and follow him. He was not sending them alone into the conflict but leading them, and asked only that they follow bravely. Even in their shock, none of them was minded to forsake him. The scene shows that the good intentions of those closest to us can at times become the greatest temptation, and that discernment is needed to recognize it.
p158.s6.b4: The apostles only vaguely grasped that he was speaking of his death; what he said about rising again failed to register at all. Yet as the days passed, Peter, James, and John, recalling the mount of transfiguration, came to understand some of these matters more fully. The experience on the mountain became a key to hard sayings later on. A deep experience need not be fully understood at the time; with time it can become a light on other stages of life.
p158.s7.h: VIII. At Peter’s House — Like a Little Child
p158.s7.b0: When they reached Capernaum, Jesus asked what they had been discussing all afternoon, and the apostles held their peace. They had been continuing the argument about rank begun at Mount Hermon. Jesus set one of Peter’s little children in their midst.

p158.s7.b1.q: Whosoever shall humble himself and become as this little one, the same shall become greatest in the kingdom of heaven.

p158.s7.b2: Jesus told the apostles that if they would be first in the kingdom, they should seek to minister these good truths to their brethren in the flesh. The teaching that the way to greatness is service echoes what they had heard in Celsus’ garden; the apostles who argued over rank heard the same lesson twice within a few days.

p158.s7.b3.q: But most of all, see that you despise not one of these little ones

p158.s7.b4: He charged them not to cause the little ones to stumble, to sacrifice the cherished idols that hinder the progress of the kingdom, and never to despise even one of these little ones. To men contending for greatness, the answer given was not exaltation but humility.
p158.s8.b0: Paper 158 sets the mountain of glory beside the valley of failure. Jesus declined universe authority and chose to live as one among men, while the apostles at his side went through rivalry, failure, and shock again and again. Yet Jesus was always patient with their human shortcomings and firm only when something threatened the doing of the Father’s will.
